summary: Learners explore why apparently costly or self-sacrificing traits evolve by redefining fitness as reproductive success. Three linked models drive the ideas: a sexual-selection trade-off (ornament cost vs mating benefit), Hamilton's rule for kin-selected altruism (rB > C), and the hawk-dove game showing a frequency-dependent evolutionarily stable strategy. A concept check and an optional debate extension cover the definition of fitness, computing rB vs C, reading payoff matrices, and the evidence question of cognitive ethology.
misconceptions: 'Animals do things for the good of the species/group' — selection favours traits raising the individual's (or its genes') reproductive success; group-selection explanations are usually wrong.
'The fittest = the strongest or longest-lived' — fitness is reproductive success; a short-lived, showy male can be fitter than a drab survivor.
'Costly ornaments are just decoration with no function' — they can be honest signals of quality or products of runaway female choice.
'Altruism disproves natural selection / animals are just being nice' — kin selection (helping relatives who share genes) explains apparent self-sacrifice quantitatively.
'There's always one single best behaviour' — the best strategy can be frequency-dependent (an ESS is a mix, not a lone winner).

activities.title: Peacock's tail: when a survival cost pays off
steps: Vary the size of a peacock's ornament and read off two quantities that change with it: a rising survival cost (slower, easier for predators to catch) and a rising mating success (peahens choose showier males).

Combine the two into a net reproductive-success curve and find where it peaks. With the model's settings, notice the peak can sit at a large, 'wasteful'-looking tail rather than a small survival-safe one.

Increase the strength of female preference and observe how the optimum tail size shifts larger. In runaway selection, the preference and the tail evolve together over generations because offspring inherit both, so this pressure can keep strengthening.

Relate the same cost-versus-mating trade-off to other sexually selected traits — bird-of-paradise courtship displays and loud frog mating calls — and note that the mating advantage can arise through female choice OR through male-male competition.
State in your own words why natural selection has NOT removed the costly tail.
activities.insight: Fitness means reproductive success, not survival or strength: a trait that lowers survival can still spread if it raises mating success enough. The same logic covers other sexually selected traits (bird-of-paradise displays, frog calls) and both routes to mating success — female choice and male-male competition. Ornaments can be honest signals of quality or products of runaway female choice, not mere decoration.

activities.title: Hamilton's rule: why a sterile worker or a sentinel helps
steps: Set a relatedness value r for the helper and the helped (e.g. full sibling r = 0.5), a benefit B to the relative, and a cost C to the helper.
Compute rB and compare it with C; decide whether the altruism gene should spread (rB > C) or die out (rB < C).

Work a model case: treat a meerkat sentinel as paying a cost C to warn relatives (benefit B shared among kin). Vary r, B and C and find the threshold where helping becomes favoured. Note that field studies suggest sentinels may face little extra risk and may also benefit themselves (for example, they often spot danger and reach cover first), so real sentinel behaviour may not be pure kin-selected altruism.
Explain why this is a gene's-eye prediction — helping copies of one's own genes carried in relatives — rather than 'for the good of the species'.
activities.insight: Apparent self-sacrifice toward relatives is a calculable prediction of inclusive fitness: an altruism gene spreads when rB > C. This replaces vague group-benefit reasoning with quantitative individual/gene-level reasoning.

activities.title: Hawk-dove game: no single best move
steps: Read a hawk-dove payoff matrix and work out what a hawk and a dove each gain when they meet a hawk and when they meet a dove.

Seed a population with a chosen starting mix of hawks and doves and let it play repeated contests. With the default payoffs set so injury cost exceeds resource value, watch the proportions settle toward a stable mixed equilibrium (the evolutionarily stable strategy).

Change the payoffs (e.g. the cost of injury in a hawk-hawk fight) and observe how the equilibrium moves — a mixed ESS when injury cost exceeds resource value, shifting toward pure hawk when it does not.

With injury cost set higher than the resource value, predict what happens when a few doves are added to a population that is almost all hawks, then test it: explain why pure aggression stops winning once almost everyone is a hawk.
activities.insight: The best behaviour can be frequency-dependent: with injury cost exceeding resource value an ESS is a stable mix, not a lone winner. 'Survival of the fittest' does not mean the strongest or most aggressive always wins — the best move depends on what everyone else is playing and on the payoff values (with a low injury cost, pure hawk can instead be favoured).

activities.title: Knowledge check: fitness, Hamilton's rule and payoffs
steps: Answer what 'fittest' means in evolution (reproductive success, not longest survival or greatest strength).
Given r, B and C values, compute rB and state whether rB > C, and hence whether helping is favoured.
Read a hawk-dove payoff matrix and identify which strategy pays better against a given opponent.
activities.insight: Consolidates the definition of fitness, the arithmetic of Hamilton's rule, and reading a payoff matrix as checkable knowledge.

activities.title: Optional debate: noble meerkat, or Hamilton's rule? (cognitive ethology extension)
steps: Argue the possible explanations for 'is the meerkat sentinel being noble, is it Hamilton's rule, or is it simply looking after itself?' and decide which explanations make testable predictions.
Examine a claim about animal emotion, play or culture and separate the evidence from the interpretation — state what observation would support or weaken the claim.
Challenge a 'for the good of the species' statement and reframe it at the individual/gene level.
activities.insight: Behavioural explanations must be evidence-based; cognitive-ethology claims about animal emotion or culture are open evidence questions, and group-benefit language can usually be recast in individual/gene-level terms.

checkQuestion: A peacock's huge, heavy tail makes it slower and easier for predators to catch — it is bad for survival. So why hasn't natural selection got rid of it? Why do peacocks still grow these extravagant tails?
checkAnswer: Because survival isn't all that counts — evolutionarily what matters is passing on genes, which needs both surviving AND mating. Peahens prefer males with big, showy tails (a costly tail can signal a healthy, high-quality male), so bigger-tailed males mate more and leave more offspring. That extra mating success outweighs the survival cost, so the trait spreads and can even run away to extremes. This is sexual selection — a form of natural selection in which mating advantage, not just survival, drives the trait.
